edits.definition: A microscope is an optical instrument that uses a combination of lenses to produce a magnified image of objects too small for the naked eye — cells, bacteria, crystals of salt, a thread of spider silk. Simple microscopes use a single convex lens (the magnifying glass), while compound microscopes pass light through the specimen and through two lens systems, the objective and the eyepiece, multiplying their magnifications. Magnification alone would be useless without resolving power — the ability to show two nearby points as separate — and together the two properties opened up the hidden world of cells and microorganisms to science.

Renewable energy resources are energy sources that nature replenishes as fast as we use them — sunlight, wind, flowing water, geothermal heat and biomass. Solar panels harvest radiation, turbines harvest wind and river flow, and the Earth's interior continuously supplies heat, so none of these draw down a finite reserve the way coal or petroleum does. They are called 'clean' for the same reason: harnessing them releases little or no carbon dioxide. The practical challenges are concentration and storage — sunlight is diffuse, the wind does not always blow — which is why renewables complement, and are steadily replacing, the finite fossil fuels.

The judiciary is the third pillar of government — the branch of courts that applies the law to disputes after the legislature makes it and the executive enforces it. Its work is adjudication: hearing civil conflicts (property, contracts, family matters) and criminal cases (offences against society's peace), weighing the evidence, and delivering judgments that bind the parties. In doing so it interprets statutes and, above all, the Constitution — which makes it also the umpire between citizen and state and the guardian of Fundamental Rights. Its independence from the other two branches, secured through secure tenures and salaries, is what lets its verdicts be impartial.

The judiciary is the institution of courts that interprets the law, settles disputes and upholds the Constitution — the arm of the state that says, finally, what the law means and whether an act of government or a citizen conforms to it. Its jurisdiction runs over civil wrongs, criminal offences and constitutional questions alike; its independence is guaranteed by the Constitution so that its decisions rest on law and evidence rather than on the wishes of the ruling party. Every right the Constitution promises — equality, freedom, protection from exploitation — becomes real only because a citizen can enforce it before a judge.
